title: Noureddin and the Fair Persian
paragraphs: Balsora was the capital of a kingdom that had long paid tribute to the caliph. In the days of the Caliph Haroun-al-Raschid, the king of Balsora, who was his cousin, was named Zinebi. Thinking one vizier not enough to run his affairs, he had two, called Khacan and Saouy.

Khacan was kind, generous and open-handed, and he took pleasure in helping, as far as he could, anyone who came to him on business. In the whole kingdom there was no one who did not respect him and speak well of him, as he deserved.

Saouy was a very different man. He put off everyone who came near him. He was always sullen, and for all his enormous wealth he was so stingy that he went without even the basic necessities of life. What made people loathe him most was his deep hatred of Khacan, whom he never stopped slandering to the king.

One day the king was relaxing in conversation with his two viziers and the other members of the council, and the talk came round to female slaves. Some argued that it was enough for a slave to be beautiful. Others, Khacan among them, held that beauty alone was not enough, and that she must also have wit, good sense and modesty, and, ideally, learning as well.

The king not only agreed with this view, he ordered Khacan to find him a slave who met all these requirements. Saouy had argued the other side, and he was jealous of the honor shown to Khacan. “Sire,” he said, “a slave as accomplished as Your Majesty wants will be very hard to find, and if there is one, she will be a bargain at anything under 10,000 gold pieces.”
“Saouy,” the king replied, “you seem to think that is a huge sum. Perhaps it is for you, but it is not for me.”
And he immediately told his grand treasurer, who was standing by, to pay 10,000 gold pieces to Khacan to buy the slave.

As soon as Khacan got home, he summoned the dealers in female slaves and told them to let him know the moment they found one who matched his description. They promised to do all they could, and not a day went by without their bringing him a slave to look over, but every one of them had some flaw.

Finally, early one morning, as Khacan was walking to the king’s palace, a dealer stepped into his path and told him excitedly that a Persian merchant, who had arrived the evening before, had a slave for sale whose wit and good sense matched her matchless beauty.

Khacan was delighted by the news and ordered that the slave be brought to him when he came back from the palace. The dealer came at the time agreed, and Khacan found the girl more beautiful than he had dared to hope. He named her “The Fair Persian” on the spot.

Khacan was a wise and educated man, and from the short talk he had with her he saw that he could search forever and find no other slave who surpassed her in any of the qualities the king demanded. So he asked the dealer what price the merchant was setting on her.

“Sir,” the dealer answered, “he will not part with her for less than 10,000 gold pieces. He says that with teachers for her schooling and her physical training, not to mention her clothes and her keep, he has already spent that much on her. She is fit in every way to be a king’s slave. She plays every musical instrument, she sings, she dances, she writes poetry. In short, there is no accomplishment in which she is not outstanding.”

Khacan was a far better judge of her worth than the dealer was, and he wanted to settle the matter quickly. He sent for the merchant and said to him, “I am not buying your slave for myself but for the king. Even so, your price is too high.”

“Sir,” the merchant replied, “I would count it an honor to give her to His Majesty as a gift, if it were proper for a merchant to do such a thing. I am asking only for what it cost me to make her what she is.”
Khacan had no wish to haggle. He had the money counted out at once and handed to the merchant, who said before leaving:

“Sir, since she is meant for the king, let me point out that she is worn out from the long journey. Before you present her to His Majesty, you would be wise to keep her in your own house for a fortnight and see that she is looked after a little. The sun has darkened her skin, but after two or three visits to the bath, and once she is properly dressed, you will see how much more beautiful she becomes.”

Khacan thanked the merchant for the advice and resolved to take it. He gave the lovely Persian rooms next to his wife’s, and told his wife to treat her as a lady destined for the king and to order the most magnificent clothes for her.

Before leaving the Fair Persian, he said to her, “No fortune could be greater than the one I have won for you. See for yourself: you now belong to the king. But I must warn you about one thing. I have a son. He is not lacking in sense, but he is young, foolish and headstrong, and I order you to keep away from him.”
The Persian thanked him for the warning and promised to heed it.

Noureddin (that was the name of the vizier’s son) came and went freely in his mother’s rooms. He was young, handsome and likeable, and he had a gift for charming everyone he met. The moment he saw the beautiful Persian, he was swept away by her charms, even though he knew she was meant for the king, and he made up his mind at once to do whatever he could to keep her for himself. The Persian was just as taken with Noureddin, and she thought to herself, “The vizier does me too great an honor by buying me for the king. I would be very happy if he gave me to his son instead.”
Noureddin took every chance he could to gaze at her beauty and to talk and laugh with her, and he would never have left her side if his mother had not made him.

Because of the long journey, the beautiful Persian had not been to the bath for some time. Five or six days after she was bought, the vizier’s wife ordered the bath to be heated for her, and told her own female slaves to attend her there and afterwards to dress her in a magnificent gown that had been prepared for her.

When she was ready, the beautiful Persian went to show herself to the vizier’s wife, who barely knew her, so much lovelier had she become. She kissed the lady’s hand and said, “Madam, I do not know what you make of me in this dress you had made for me. Your women tell me it suits me so well that they hardly recognized me. If they are telling me the truth and not just flattering me, then I owe the change to you.”

“My daughter,” the vizier’s wife answered, “they are not flattering you. I hardly knew you myself. It is not only the dress, but mostly the effect of the bath. I am so struck by the result that I want to try it myself.”
She acted on this at once. While she was away, she told two young slave girls to keep watch over the beautiful Persian and not to let Noureddin in if he came.

She had barely left when he arrived. He did not find his mother in her rooms and was going to look for her in the Persian’s. The two girls blocked the way and said his mother had ordered that he must not be admitted. He took each of them by the arm, pushed them out of the anteroom and shut the door. They ran to the bath and told their mistress, shrieking and in tears, that Noureddin had thrown them out by force and gone in.

The lady was thrown into alarm by this news. She dressed as fast as she could and hurried to the fair Persian’s rooms, only to find that Noureddin had already left. The Persian was very surprised to see the vizier’s wife come in weeping, and asked what disaster had happened.
“What!” cried the lady. “You ask me that, when you know my son Noureddin has been alone with you?”
“But madam,” said the Persian, “what is wrong with that?”
“What do you mean? Did my husband not tell you that you are meant for the king?”

“He did, but Noureddin has just come to tell me that his father has changed his mind and given me to him. I believed him, and I am so fond of Noureddin that I would gladly spend my whole life with him.”
“Heaven grant that what you say were true,” cried the vizier’s wife. “But Noureddin has deceived you, and his father will put him to death for what he has done.”
With these words she wept bitterly, and all her slaves wept with her.

Khacan came in soon afterwards and was astonished to find his wife and her slaves in tears and the beautiful Persian deeply upset. He asked what was wrong, but for a while no one answered. When his wife had calmed down enough to tell him what had happened, his rage and shame knew no limits. He wrung his hands and tore at his beard, crying out:

“Wretched boy! You are destroying not only yourself but your father. The king will spill your blood, and mine too.” His wife tried to comfort him. “Don’t torment yourself,” she said. “I will sell my jewels to raise 10,000 gold pieces, and you can buy another slave with that.”

“Don’t imagine,” her husband replied, “that it is the loss of the money that troubles me. It is my honor that is at stake, and that matters more to me than all my wealth. You know Saouy is my sworn enemy. He will tell the king everything, and you will see what comes of it.”

“My lord,” said his wife, “I know very well how base Saouy is, and that he is quite capable of playing this spiteful trick on you. But how could he or anyone else know what goes on in this house? Even if the king suspects you and accuses you, you need only say that you examined the slave and found her unworthy of His Majesty. Put your mind at rest. Send word to the dealers that you are not satisfied and want them to find you another slave.”

Khacan thought this advice sensible and decided to follow it, but his anger at his son did not fade. Noureddin did not dare show himself all that day. He was afraid to go to his usual companions in case his father looked for him there, so he spent the day in a remote garden where no one knew him. He came home only after his father had gone to bed, and left early the next morning before the vizier woke. He kept up these precautions for a whole month.
His mother knew perfectly well that he came back to the house every evening, but she did not dare ask her husband to forgive him. In the end she found her courage and said:

“My lord, I know that no son could behave more shamefully toward his father than Noureddin has toward you. But will you not forgive him now? Do you not see the harm you may be doing to yourself? Do you not fear that spiteful people, looking for the reason you have turned against him, may guess the true one?”
“Madam,” the vizier replied, “what you say is quite right, but I cannot forgive Noureddin until I have humbled him as he deserves.”

“He will be punished enough,” the lady answered, “if you do what I suggest. This evening, when he comes home, lie in wait for him and pretend you mean to kill him. I will come to his rescue. You can tell him that you spare his life only because of my pleading, and then you can make him take the beautiful Persian on whatever terms you like.” Khacan agreed to follow this plan, and it all went as arranged. When Noureddin came home, Khacan pretended he was about to kill him, but then gave way to his wife’s entreaties and said to his son:

“You owe your life to your mother. I forgive you because she asked me to, on these conditions: that you take the beautiful Persian as your wife, not your slave, and that you never sell her or send her away.”

Noureddin had not hoped for such leniency. He thanked his father and swore to do as he was told. Khacan took care to speak to the king often about the difficulties of the task he had been given, but some whispers of what had really happened did reach Saouy’s ears.

More than a year after these events, the minister caught a chill when he left the bath still overheated to go out on urgent business. It turned into an inflammation of the lungs, and it quickly grew worse. The vizier felt his end was near. He sent for Noureddin, and with his dying breath ordered him never to part with the beautiful Persian.

He died soon afterwards, and the whole kingdom mourned him; rich and poor alike followed him to the grave. Noureddin showed every sign of the deepest grief at his father’s death and for a long time refused to see anyone. At last the day came when a friend, who was let in, urged him strongly to take comfort and return to his old place in society. Noureddin was quick to take the advice. Soon he had gathered a little circle of ten young men about his own age, and he spent all his time with them in constant feasting and merrymaking.

Sometimes the fair Persian agreed to appear at these parties, but she disapproved of the extravagant spending and did not hesitate to warn Noureddin where it would lead. He only laughed at her advice. He said his father had always kept him under too tight a rein, and now he was delighted to be free.
Making matters worse for his finances, he refused to go over his accounts with his steward, and sent the man away every time he came with his book.
“Just make sure I live well,” he said, “and don’t bother me about anything else.”

Noureddin’s friends were not only always at his table; they took advantage of his generosity in every way they could. Whatever of his they admired, whether land, houses, baths or any other source of income, he gave to them on the spot. The Persian protested in vain that he was wronging himself. He went on scattering his wealth with the same open hand.

For one whole year Noureddin did nothing but enjoy himself and squander the fortune his father had worked so hard to build. The year had barely ended when, one day as they sat at dinner, there was a knock at the door. The slaves had been sent away, so Noureddin went to open it himself. One of his friends had got up at the same moment, but Noureddin reached the door first. He found that the caller was the steward, stepped outside and closed the door behind him. The friend, curious to hear what passed between them, hid behind the hangings and overheard these words:

“My lord,” said the steward, “I beg your pardon a thousand times for interrupting you, but what I have long feared has happened. Nothing is left of the money you gave me for your expenses, and your other sources of income are gone too, because you have given them away to others. If you want me to stay in your service, give me the funds I need. Otherwise I must leave.”
Noureddin was so shocked that he could not find a word to answer.
The friend, who had been listening behind the curtain, hurried straight back to tell the rest of the company the news.
“If that is so,” they said, “we must stop coming here.”

Noureddin came back in at that moment, and in spite of his efforts to hide it, they could plainly see that what they had heard was true. One by one they got up and left the room, each with a different excuse, until he found himself alone, with no idea of the decision his friends had made. Then he saw the beautiful Persian and told her what the steward had said, with many expressions of regret for his own carelessness.

“If I had only taken your advice, beautiful Persian,” he said, “none of this would have happened. Still, I have one comfort: I went through my fortune among friends who will stand by me when I need them. Tomorrow I will visit them, and between them they will lend me enough to set up in some business.”

So early the next morning Noureddin set out to find his ten friends, all of whom lived on the same street. He knocked at the door of the first, the chief among them. The slave who answered left him waiting in a hall while he went to tell his master who had come. Noureddin heard him quite clearly: “Noureddin!” the master cried. “Tell him, every time he calls, that I am not at home.” The same happened at the second door, and at the third, and so on through all ten. Noureddin was deeply humiliated. Too late, he saw that he had trusted false friends, who had dropped him the moment he needed them. Heavy with grief, he went back to the beautiful Persian to be comforted.
“Alas, my lord,” she said, “now you see that what I warned you of was true. The only thing left to you is to sell your slaves and your furniture.”

So he sold the slaves first and lived on the money for a while. Then the furniture went, and since much of it was valuable, that lasted him some time too. At last this source also ran dry, and once more he asked the beautiful Persian what he should do.

“My lord,” she said, “I know that the late vizier, your father, paid 10,000 gold pieces for me. I may be worth less now than I was then, but I would still bring a large sum. So do not hesitate to sell me. Take what you get for me and go set yourself up in business in some faraway town.”
“Charming Persian,” Noureddin answered, “how could I do something so base? I would sooner die than be parted from you, whom I love more than my own life.”
“My lord,” she replied, “I know well how much you love me, and I love you just as much. But harsh necessity forces us to take the only remedy there is.”

In the end Noureddin was convinced by her words. He gave in, and with heavy reluctance led her to the slave market. There he pointed her out to a dealer named Hagi Hassan and asked what she was worth.
Hagi Hassan took the two of them into a private room. As soon as she lifted her veil he cried out, “My lord, isn’t this the slave your father bought for 10,000 pieces?”

Learning that it was, he promised to get the best price possible for her. He left the beautiful Persian shut in the room by herself and went out to find the slave merchants, telling them he had found the pearl of all slaves and inviting them to come and name her value. The moment they saw her, they agreed that the asking price could not be less than 4,000 gold pieces. Hagi Hassan then closed the door on her and began the sale, calling out, “Who will bid 4,000 gold pieces for the Persian slave?”

Before any merchant had made a bid, Saouy happened to ride by. He guessed that this must be a slave of rare beauty, so he rode up to Hagi Hassan and demanded to see her. It was not the custom to show a slave to a single private buyer, but nobody dared defy the vizier, so he got what he asked for.

The moment Saouy saw the Persian, her beauty struck him so hard that he wanted her for himself at once. He did not know she belonged to Noureddin, and he told Hagi Hassan to send for the owner and settle the bargain on the spot.

Hagi Hassan went to find Noureddin. He told him that his slave was about to go for far less than she was worth, and that if Saouy bought her, he might well never pay. “Here is what you must do,” he said. “Pretend you never really meant to sell her, and that you only swore you would in a fit of anger at her. When I present her to Saouy as though you agreed, step in and start dragging her away with blows.”

Noureddin did as Hagi Hassan had advised. Saouy was furious, and rode straight at him to take the beautiful Persian by force. Noureddin let go of her, caught Saouy’s horse by the bridle, and, cheered on by the crowd, pulled him to the ground, beat him badly, and left him in the gutter streaming with blood. Then he took the beautiful Persian and went home among the cheers of the people. They hated Saouy so much that they would neither step in on his behalf nor let his slaves defend him.

Saouy got up, covered with filth from head to foot and streaming with blood. Leaning on two of his slaves, he went straight to the palace and asked to be received by the king. When he was, he told what had happened in these words:

“May it please your Majesty, I had gone to the slave market to buy myself a cook. While I was there, I heard a slave being offered at 4,000 pieces. I asked to see her and found she was incomparably beautiful. The seller was Noureddin, the son of your late vizier. Your Majesty may remember giving his father 10,000 gold pieces to buy a slave. This is that very slave. Instead of bringing her to your Majesty, he gave her to his own son. Since his father died, this Noureddin has gone through his whole fortune and sold everything he owned, and now he is reduced to selling the slave. I called him over and said, ‘Noureddin, I will give you 10,000 gold pieces for your slave, and I will present her to the king. At the same time I will speak to him in your favor, and that will be worth far more to you than any extra money you might get from the merchants.’ ‘Wicked old man,’ he shouted, ‘I would give her to a Jew before I would sell her to you!’ ‘But Noureddin,’ I protested, ‘don’t you see that speaking this way wrongs the king, to whom your father owed everything?’ My protest only made him angrier. He threw himself on me like a madman, tore me from my horse, beat me to his heart’s content, and left me in the state your Majesty sees.”
With that, Saouy turned his head away and wept bitterly.

The king was filled with rage against Noureddin. He ordered the captain of the guard to take forty men, plunder Noureddin’s house, tear it down to the ground, and bring Noureddin and the slave before him. A doorkeeper named Sangiar, who had once been a slave of Khacan’s, heard the order given. He slipped out of the king’s apartment and hurried to warn Noureddin to flee at once with the beautiful Persian. Then he pressed forty gold pieces into his hand and vanished before Noureddin could even thank him.

As soon as the fair Persian had put on her veil, the two fled together, and by good luck they got out of the town unseen. At the mouth of the Euphrates they found a ship just about to leave for Baghdad. They went aboard, and straight away the anchor was raised and the ship set sail.

When the captain of the guard reached Noureddin’s house, he had his soldiers break down the door and force their way in. They found no trace of Noureddin or his slave, and the neighbors could tell them nothing. When the king heard they had escaped, he issued a proclamation: anyone who brought him Noureddin and the slave would receive a reward of 1,000 gold pieces, and anyone who hid them would be severely punished. Meanwhile Noureddin and the fair Persian had arrived safely in Baghdad. When the vessel dropped anchor, they paid five gold pieces for their passage and went ashore. They had never been in Baghdad before and did not know where to look for lodging. As they wandered along the bank of the Tigris, they came to a garden surrounded by a high wall. The gate was shut, but in front of it was an open porch with a sofa on each side. “Let us spend the night here,” said Noureddin. They lay down on the sofas and were soon asleep.

This garden belonged to the Caliph. In the middle of it stood a huge pavilion with a magnificent hall that had eighty windows, and each window had a lamp that was lit only when the Caliph spent an evening there. The only person who lived there was the doorkeeper, an old soldier named Scheih Ibrahim. He had strict orders to be very careful about whom he let in, and never to let anyone sit on the sofas by the door. That evening he happened to be out on an errand. When he came back and found two people asleep on the sofas, he was about to chase them off with blows. But as he came closer he saw a handsome young man and a beautiful young woman, and decided to wake them more gently. When Noureddin woke, he told the old man they were strangers who only wanted to spend the night there. “Come with me,” said Scheih Ibrahim. “I will find you better lodging, and I will show you a wonderful garden of mine.” With these words the doorkeeper led them into the Caliph’s garden, and its beauty filled them with wonder and amazement. Noureddin took out two gold pieces, handed them to Scheih Ibrahim, and said,

“Please get us something to eat, so that we can make merry together.” Scheih Ibrahim was very greedy, and decided to spend only a tenth of the money and keep the rest for himself. While he was away, Noureddin and the Persian strolled through the gardens and climbed the white marble staircase of the pavilion as far as the locked door of the hall. When Scheih Ibrahim returned, they asked him to open it and let them go in and admire the splendor inside. He agreed, fetched not only the key but also a light, and unlocked the door at once. Noureddin and the Persian went in and were dazzled by what they saw. The paintings and furnishings were astonishingly beautiful, and between each pair of windows was a silver arm holding a candle.
Scheih Ibrahim laid out a meal in front of a sofa, and the three of them ate together. When they had finished, Noureddin asked the old man to bring a bottle of wine.
“Heaven forbid,” said Scheih Ibrahim, “that I should have anything to do with wine! I have made the pilgrimage to Mecca four times, and I gave up wine for good.”

“Still, you would do us a great favor by getting us some,” said Noureddin. “You needn’t touch it yourself. Take the donkey tied up at the gate and lead it to the nearest wine shop. Ask a passer-by to order two jars of wine, have them loaded into the donkey’s panniers, and drive it back in front of you. Here are two gold pieces to pay for it.”

The sight of the gold sent Scheih Ibrahim off at once to carry out the errand. When he came back, Noureddin said, “We still need cups to drink from, and some fruit, if you can find any.” Scheih Ibrahim vanished again and soon returned with a table laid with gold and silver cups and every kind of fine fruit. Then he left, though they begged him again and again to stay.

Noureddin and the beautiful Persian found the wine excellent and drank it freely, and as they drank they sang. They both had fine voices, and Scheih Ibrahim listened with great pleasure. At first he stayed at a distance, then he crept closer, and finally he put his head in at the door. Noureddin saw him and called him in to keep them company. At first the old man refused, but they persuaded him to come in, to sit on the edge of the sofa nearest the door, and in the end to move closer and sit beside the beautiful Persian. She pressed him so insistently to drink her health that at last he gave in and took the cup she held out.

In truth, the old man only pretended to have given up wine. He went to wine shops like anyone else, and he had taken none of the precautions Noureddin had suggested. Once he had given in, it was easy to talk him into a second cup, then a third, and so on until he no longer knew what he was doing. They went on drinking, laughing, and singing together until nearly midnight.

Around that time the Persian saw that the only light in the room came from a single miserable tallow candle, and she asked Scheih Ibrahim to light a few of the lovely candles standing in the silver arms.
“Light them yourself,” the old man answered. “You are younger than I am. But five or six will be plenty.”
She did not stop until she had lit all eighty, but Scheih Ibrahim was in no state to notice it. Shortly afterward, when Noureddin proposed lighting some of the lamps as well, he answered:
“You can do it better than I can, but no more than three.”
Noureddin was far from content with three. He lit them all and threw open all eighty windows.

At that moment the Caliph Haroun-al-Raschid happened to open a window in the hall of his palace that looked out over the garden, and was amazed to see the pavilion blazing with light. He called for the grand vizier, Giafar, and said to him:
“Careless vizier, look at the pavilion and tell me why it is lit up when I am not there.”
When the vizier saw that it was just as the Caliph said, he shook with fear and quickly made up an excuse.

“Commander of the Faithful,” he said, “I must tell you that four or five days ago Scheih Ibrahim told me he wanted to hold a gathering of the officials of his mosque, and asked my permission to hold it in the pavilion. I gave it, but I have forgotten until now to mention it to your Majesty.”

“Giafar,” replied the Caliph, “you have made three mistakes. First, you gave the permission. Second, you did not tell me. Third, you did not look into the matter more carefully. As your punishment, I sentence you to spend the rest of the night with me in the company of these worthy people. While I dress as a commoner, go and disguise yourself, and then come with me.”

When they reached the garden gate, they found it open, which made the Caliph very angry. The door of the pavilion was open too. He went quietly upstairs and looked through the half-closed door of the hall. He was astonished to see Scheih Ibrahim, whose sobriety he had never doubted, drinking and singing with a young man and a beautiful lady. Before giving way to anger, the Caliph decided to watch and find out who these people were and what they were doing.
After a while Scheih Ibrahim asked the beautiful Persian whether anything was missing that would make her evening complete.
“If only,” she said, “I had an instrument that I could play.”

Scheih Ibrahim took a lute from a cupboard at once and gave it to the Persian. She began to play and sing along with such skill and taste that the Caliph was enchanted. When she stopped, he went quietly downstairs and said to the vizier:
“I have never heard a finer voice, or a lute better played. I am determined to go in and have her play for me.”
“Commander of the Faithful,” said the vizier, “if Scheih Ibrahim recognizes you, he will die of fright.”
“I would be sorry for that,” answered the Caliph, “and I am going to make sure it does not happen. Wait here until I come back.”

The Caliph had had a bend of the river turned into a lake in his garden. The finest fish of the Tigris were to be found there, but fishing was strictly forbidden. That night, though, a fisherman had taken advantage of the open gate to slip in and cast his nets. He was just about to haul them in when he saw the Caliph coming. He knew him at once despite the disguise, and threw himself at his feet, begging forgiveness.
“Don’t be afraid,” said the Caliph. “Just get up and pull in your nets.”

The fisherman did as he was told and hauled up five or six fine fish. The Caliph kept the two biggest and asked the fisherman to swap clothes with him. Within minutes the Caliph had become a fisherman from his shoes to his turban. With the two fish in his hand he went back to the vizier, who failed to recognize him and would have sent him packing. The Caliph left the vizier at the foot of the stairs, climbed up, and knocked at the door of the hall. Noureddin opened it, and the Caliph, standing on the threshold, said:
“Scheih Ibrahim, I am Kerim the fisherman. I see you are feasting with your friends, so I’ve brought you these fish.”

Noureddin and the Persian replied that once the fish had been properly cooked and prepared, they would be glad to eat them. So the Caliph went back to the vizier, and the two of them set about cooking the fish in Scheih Ibrahim’s house. They made it such a tempting dish that Noureddin and the fair Persian ate it with real enjoyment. When they had finished, Noureddin took out thirty gold pieces, everything he had left of what Sangiar had given him, and handed them to the Caliph. The Caliph thanked him and asked one more favor: would the lady play him a piece on the lute? The Persian agreed gladly, and her singing and playing delighted the Caliph.
Noureddin was in the habit of giving away anything that others admired. “Fisherman,” he said, “since she pleases you so much, take her. She is yours.”
The fair Persian was stunned that he would give her up. She picked up her lute and, with tears in her eyes, sang her reproaches to its music.
The Caliph, still playing the fisherman, said to him, “Sir, I can see that this fair lady is your slave. Please do me the kindness of telling me your story.”
Noureddin readily agreed, and told him everything, from the day he bought the slave to the present moment.
“And where are you going now?” asked the Caliph.
“Wherever the hand of Allah takes me,” said Noureddin.
“Then listen to me,” said the Caliph. “Go back to Balsora at once. I will give you a letter for the king, and it will win you a warm welcome from him.”
“It’s unheard of,” said Noureddin, “for a fisherman to write letters to a king.”
“Don’t let that surprise you,” answered the Caliph. “We studied together and have always stayed the best of friends, though fortune made him a king and left me a humble fisherman.”

The Caliph then took a sheet of paper and wrote the following letter. At the very top, in tiny characters, he put a formula showing that it must be obeyed without question: “In the name of the Most Merciful God.
“Letter from the Caliph Haroun-al-Raschid to the King of Balsora.

“Haroun-al-Raschid, son of Mahdi, sends this letter to his cousin Mohammed Zinebi. As soon as Noureddin, son of the Vizier Khacan, who carries this letter, hands it to you and you have read it, take off your royal mantle, place it on his shoulders, and seat him in your place. Do not fail in this. Farewell.”

The Caliph handed the letter to Noureddin, who set off at once with nothing but the little money he had had before Sangiar came to his aid. The beautiful Persian, inconsolable at his departure, sank onto a sofa and wept.

After Noureddin had left the room, Scheih Ibrahim, who had kept silent until then, said, “Kerim, for two wretched fish you have been given a purse and a slave. Here is what I say: I will take the slave. As for the purse, if it holds silver you may keep one piece, and if it holds gold I will take the lot and give you whatever copper I have in my own purse.”

Now it must be told here that when the Caliph went upstairs with the plate of fish, he had ordered the vizier to hurry to the palace and return with four slaves carrying a change of clothes. They were to wait outside the pavilion until the Caliph clapped his hands.

Still acting the fisherman, the Caliph answered, “Scheih Ibrahim, I will split whatever is in the purse equally with you, but the slave I keep for myself. If you won’t accept those terms, you get nothing.”

The old man, furious at what he took for insolence, snatched up a cup and flung it at the Caliph. The Caliph easily dodged a missile thrown by a drunken hand, and the cup struck the wall and smashed into a thousand pieces. Scheih Ibrahim, angrier still, went out to fetch a stick. At that moment the Caliph clapped his hands, and the vizier and the four slaves came in, stripped off the fisherman’s clothes, and dressed him in those they had brought.

When Scheih Ibrahim came back with a thick stick in his hand, the Caliph was sitting on his throne, and all that remained of the fisherman was a heap of clothes in the middle of the room. Scheih Ibrahim threw himself to the ground at the Caliph’s feet and said, “Commander of the Faithful, your miserable slave has offended you and begs your forgiveness.”

The Caliph stepped down from his throne and said, “Get up. I forgive you.” Then he turned to the Persian and said, “Fair lady, now you know who I am. Know this as well: I have sent Noureddin to Balsora to be its king, and once all the preparations are made I will send you there to be its queen. Until then I will give you rooms in my palace, where you will be treated with every honor.”
At this the beautiful Persian took heart, and the Caliph kept his word, placing her in the care of his wife Zobeida.

Noureddin hurried on his journey to Balsora. As soon as he arrived he went straight to the king’s palace and asked for an audience, which was granted at once. Holding the letter high above his head, he pushed his way through the crowd. As the king read it, his face changed color. He would have carried out the Caliph’s order on the spot, but first he showed the letter to Saouy, whose interests were at stake just as much as his own. Saouy pretended he wanted to read it a second time and stepped aside as though looking for better light. Unseen by anyone, he tore the formula off the top of the letter, put it in his mouth, and swallowed it. Then he turned to the king and said:

“Your majesty has no need to obey this letter. The handwriting is certainly the Caliph’s, but the formula is missing. Besides, he has not sent a messenger with the patent, and without it the letter is worthless. Leave everything to me, and I will take the consequences.”

The king not only let Saouy persuade him but handed Noureddin over to him. Noureddin was first given such a savage beating on the soles of his feet that he was left more dead than alive. Then Saouy threw him into the darkest, deepest dungeon and fed him on nothing but bread and water. After ten days Saouy decided to end Noureddin’s life, but he did not dare without the king’s permission. To get it, he loaded several of his own slaves with rich gifts and went at their head to the king, saying they were presents from the new king on his coronation.
“What!” said the king. “Is that wretch still alive? Go and behead him at once. You have my authority.”

“Sire,” said Saouy, “I thank your Majesty for the justice you do me. Since Noureddin insulted me in public, I would ask one thing more: that the execution take place in front of the palace, and that it be announced throughout the city so that no one can be ignorant of it.”

The king granted these requests, and the announcement caused grief everywhere, for the memory of Noureddin’s father was still fresh in the people’s hearts. Saouy went to the prison with twenty of his own slaves to fetch Noureddin, and set him on a wretched horse without a saddle. At the palace, Saouy went in to the king and left Noureddin standing in the square. He was hemmed in by Saouy’s slaves and by the royal guard, who had great trouble keeping the crowd from rushing in to rescue him. The anger against Saouy was so great that if anyone had made the first move, he would have been stoned on his way through the streets. Saouy watched the unrest of the people from the windows of the king’s private chambers and called to the executioner to strike at once. The king, however, ordered him to wait. He was jealous of Saouy’s meddling, and he had another reason too. At that very moment a troop of horsemen was seen galloping at full speed toward the square. Saouy suspected who they were and urged the king to give the signal for the execution immediately, but the king refused until he knew who the horsemen were.

They were the vizier Giafar and his company, arriving at top speed from Baghdad. For several days after Noureddin left with the letter, the Caliph had forgotten to send the messenger with the patent, without which the letter was worthless. Then one day he heard a beautiful voice uttering laments in the women’s part of the palace. He was told it was the voice of the fair Persian, and suddenly he remembered the patent. He sent for Giafar and ordered him to make for Balsora as fast as he could. If Noureddin was dead, he was to hang Saouy. If Noureddin was still alive, he was to bring him straight back to Baghdad, together with the king and Saouy.

Giafar rode at full speed through the square and dismounted at the palace steps, where the king came out to greet him. The vizier’s first question was whether Noureddin was still alive. The king said that he was, and Noureddin was brought out at once, bound hand and foot. On the vizier’s orders his bonds were removed immediately, and Saouy was tied up with the same cords. The next day Giafar went back to Baghdad, taking with him the king, Saouy, and Noureddin.

When the Caliph learned how Noureddin had been treated, he gave him leave to behead Saouy with his own hands. Noureddin refused to shed his enemy’s blood, and Saouy was handed over to the executioner straight away. The Caliph also wanted Noureddin to rule Balsora, but he refused this too. After all that had happened there, he said, he never wanted to go back, and he asked instead to enter the Caliph’s service. He became one of the Caliph’s closest courtiers and lived for many years in great happiness with the fair Persian. As for the king, the Caliph was content to send him back to Balsora with the advice to take more care in future over his choice of vizier.
